newsitem.title: THAILAND: FORECAST-Analysts see fall in Thai foreign reserves.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Analysts see fall in Thai foreign reserves.

text.p: Economists and analysts expect Thai June foreign reserves figures to fall to between $25-31 billion from $33.3 billion in May following a currency war the authorities waged with baht speculators.

The much-awaited key monthly data will be released on Thursday by the Bank of Thailand, which is believed to have spent hefty sums from its foreign reserves to defend the baht in May and June before it was floated on July 2.
Since the float the baht has slid by more than 20 percent.

Analysts also expect to see another set of disappointing overall economic indicators from the central bank pointing to a shaky external balance and stagnant investment activity in Thailand, which is facing its worst slump in over a decade.

Analysts projected the June balance of payments deficit to widen further, by 60-100 billion baht ($1.9 billion-$3.2 billion) from 112.3 billion baht in May, due to massive capital outflows triggered by a loss of investor confidence in the tottering economy.
Thailand has confirmed it is seeking International Monetary Fund advice and possibly financial assistance to help put its chronically ill economy on an even keel.
Despite the expected negative outlook, especially in the external balance picture, some analysts said the impact of the figures on sentiment would be limited.

"These figures are considered outdated given the fact that a de facto (baht) devaluation introduced in July could change the whole picture," said Arporn Chewakrenkai, chief economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfrell.

"Most of the figures will be discounted. We believe the balance of payments deficit must have risen high enough and foreign reserves dwindled to such a level that forced the government to float the baht," she added.
The Bank of Thailand will also issue fresh data on the current account, government cash balance, May trade balance, manufacturing production and private investment indices.
The trade balance was expected to improve substantially.
According to a Reuters survey, analysts' expectations of the May trade deficit ranged anywhere from 17.0-37.8 billion baht from 41 billion baht in April.
Song Seng Wun, regional economist at ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett, forecast that May exports would rise 5.5 percent year-on-year while imports would fall 3.0 percent in the same period.
But Arporn predicted that any sharp drop in the trade deficit was likely to be caused by a substantial drop in imports rather than a turnaround in exports.
"We see exports growing one percent year-on-year to 124 billion baht. Imports are likely to drop by 10 percent to 141 billion baht," she said.
A senior economist at one major U.S. investment bank said he would pay more attention to the level of investment activity.
"We are more interested to see if the activities have picked up although I have my doubts given high interest rates and dented domestic demand," he said.

Thailand's April manufacturing production index and the private investment index both rose 5.4 percent from the same month last year, down from 6.4 percent and 5.8 percent respectively a month earlier. ($ = 31.5 Thai Baht)
